entries.meaning: Kaikeyī lamented, ‘I would rather return to my parental home and spend my life there than live serving a co-wife. For one whom Fate keeps alive under an enemy's control, death is better than such a desired life.’ Hearing the queen's many humble words, the hunchback resolved to deploy feminine wiles. ‘Why speak thus and think yourself deficient? Your happiness and marital fortune will double daily. Whoever wishes you extreme harm will receive this fully ripened fruit. Since I heard of this evil plan, mistress, I have had no hunger by day and no sleep by night. I asked astrologers and they drew their calculations: it is true that Bharata will become king. If you will act, lady, I shall tell the means. The king is under the influence of serving you.’ Kaikeyī declared, ‘I would fall into a well at your word; I can abandon son and husband. Seeing my great suffering, how could you fail to act for my welfare?’

Kaikeyī accepted the hunchback's counsel and sharpened the knife of deceit upon the stone of her heart. The queen did not perceive the suffering close at hand, as a sacrificial animal grazing green grass does not see what approaches. The words sounded soft but were hard at their end, like honey mixed with poison. The maid asked, ‘Do you remember, mistress, or not? Tell me the account. Two boons are held in trust with the king. Ask for them today and cool your heart: give the kingdom to your son and forest exile to Rāma, thus taking away all your co-wife's joy. When the king swears by Rāma, then ask; he will not evade that promise. If this night passes, the undertaking will fail. Accept my words, dear one, as dearer than life.’ Having contrived the great treacherous blow, the sinner told her to go to the chamber of anger: ‘Accomplish the task while alert; do not suddenly trust everything.’

The queen regarded the hunchback as dear as life and repeatedly praised her great intelligence: ‘There is no well-wisher like you in my world. I was being swept away and you became my support. If Fate fulfils my former wish tomorrow, friend, I shall make you the pupil of my eye.’ After honouring the maid in many ways, Kaikeyī entered the chamber of anger. The maid was the seed of calamity and the rainy season; Kaikeyī's ill judgment became the soil. Receiving the water of deceit, the sprout emerged: the two boons were its leaves and sorrow its final fruit. She arranged the entire display of anger and, while ruling, ruined herself through her own bad counsel. Noise filled the king's city, but no one knew anything of this intrigue. Delighted men and women throughout the city arranged every auspicious observance. Some entered and others departed through the crowded royal court.

Hearing the news, Rāma's childhood companions rejoiced in their hearts and went to him in groups of five or ten. Recognizing their love, the Lord honoured them and gently asked after their welfare. Receiving their beloved friend's permission, they returned home while praising Rāma to one another: ‘Who in the world is like Rāma, faithful in conduct and affection? In whatever birth we wander through the force of deeds, may God grant that Rāma and Sītā be our masters and we their servants; may this bond endure from both sides.’ Everyone in the city cherished this wish, while Kaikeyī's heart burned intensely. Who is not destroyed after falling into bad company? Cleverness does not remain under the counsel of the base. At evening the happy king went to Kaikeyī's residence. It was as if embodied affection had deliberately approached embodied cruelty.

Hearing she was in the chamber of anger, the king became uneasy; under fear, his foot could not advance. All kings obeyed his inclination and Indra dwelt secure through the power of his arms, yet at news of his wife's anger he withered—behold the greatness of Love's power. Those before whom tridents, thunderbolts and swords recoiled were struck by the flower-arrows of Love's lord. Afraid, the king went to his beloved; seeing her state, he felt terrible sorrow. She lay on the ground in coarse old cloth, having thrown from her body every ornament. How aptly the ugly dress suited her bad intent, as though the future widowhood of other women were being foretold. Drawing near, the king gently asked, ‘Beloved as life, why are you angry?’

The king asked, ‘Beloved, who has harmed you? Who has two heads that Yama wishes to take? Tell me which pauper I should make king, or which king I should exile from his land. I can even kill an immortal who is your enemy—what then of wretched insects, men and women? Lovely-browed one, you know my nature: my mind is a cakora bird for the moon of your face. Beloved, life, sons and all I possess—family and subjects—are under your control. If I say anything deceitfully to you, lady, I swear by Rāma that it is true. Smile and ask for what delights your mind; adorn your charming body with ornaments. Consider in your heart whether the hour is good or bad, and quickly abandon this ugly dress.’ Hearing this, reflecting on the great oath, the dull-minded woman rose laughing. Watching her put on ornaments was like a deer watching the huntress's snare.

Again the king, believing her a friend in his heart, spoke tenderly, beautifully and with a body thrilled by love: ‘Lady, what pleases your heart has occurred; joy and congratulations fill every house in the city. Tomorrow I shall give Rāma the heirship. Beautiful-eyed one, arrange the auspicious decorations.’ Hearing this, her hard heart split open as if a ripe boil had been touched, yet she laughed and concealed even that pain, like a female thief who does not openly weep. The king did not perceive her skilful deceit, though she had studied under a teacher whose jewel held crores of crooked arts. Although the king was skilled in statecraft, he could not fathom the ocean of a woman's conduct. Increasing her deceptive affection, she turned her eyes and face away, smiled, and said: ‘Ask, ask—but beloved, you never give. You only say “take”; even the two boons you promised remain doubtful to receive.’

Understanding her meaning, the king laughed: ‘You are extremely fond of becoming angry. You left the boons in trust and never asked for them; in my guileless nature I forgot. Do not blame me even falsely. Ask four boons instead of two, if you wish. The custom of Raghu's line has always prevailed: life may go, but a pledged word does not. No heap of sin equals falsehood; can crores of guñjā seeds equal a mountain? Truth is the root of every beautiful merit, proclaimed by the Vedas and Purāṇas and sung by Manu. Above all, the oath by Rāma has come from my lips—Rāma is the limit of merit and affection.’ Having made the promise firm, the malicious woman smiled and spoke, as though she opened the cage of a flock of evil birds of bad counsel. The king's hope was a lovely forest, filled with the happy society of good birds; like a Bhīl huntress she prepared to release the dreadful hawk of her words upon it.

Kaikeyī said, ‘Hear, beloved as life, and give what pleases my heart. As one boon, anoint Bharata. I ask the second with joined hands; fulfil my wish, Lord: Rāma shall live in the forest for fourteen years, especially detached and dressed as an ascetic.’ Hearing the gentle words, grief filled the king's heart, as a cakravāka bird is distraught when touched by the moon's rays. He became stunned and no words came, like a quail struck in the forest by a falcon. The king turned utterly pale, as if a palmyra tree had been struck by lightning. He placed his hand upon his forehead, closed both eyes, and embodied Anxiety itself seemed to take form and contemplate. ‘My wish was a flowering wish-fulfilling tree, but just as it began to fruit, an elephant uprooted it.’ Kaikeyī had devastated Ayodhyā and built an immovable mechanism of calamity. ‘On what occasion has this happened? Why did I trust a woman?’ It was like ignorance destroying an ascetic just when the fruit of yogic attainment had ripened.

While the king grieved inwardly in this way, the malicious woman, seeing his bad state, became angry in mind: ‘Is Bharata not your son? Or did you buy me for a price and bring me here? If hearing this arrow-like request causes you such pain, why do you not speak carefully? Answer: will you carry out your pledge or not? You are truth-bound in Raghu's line. You said you would give, but now do not give the boon; abandon truth and take infamy in the world. Praising truth, you promised the boon because you expected me to ask only for roasted grain. Whatever Śibi, Dadhīci and Bali pledged, they abandoned body and wealth but kept their vow.’ Kaikeyī's intensely bitter words were like salt rubbed into a burn. The steadfast bearer of dharma gathered courage and opened his eyes. The king struck his head, drew a sigh and said, ‘You have struck me in a mortal place.’
